I am looking for updated, real-world feedback on the viability of various transport setups for reliable, sustained daily usage from China.

~~To be clear, I’m approaching this from the assumption that anything that has ever been broken, blocked, throttled, or fingerprinted in the past, whether by real-world deployments or formal analysis (e.g., in academic papers or widespread user reports), should not be considered as a the primaries means to circumvent censorship or bloackage unless it has since been fixed or fundamentally redesigned.~~

* **[Xray-core](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core) (`v26.11.9`)**
Under sustained daily high-bandwidth usage from China: (1) which `XHTTP + XMUX + vless-enc` tuning (`alpn: ["h3"]` vs. `["h2"]`, `XMUX` reuse limits, and `extra` header/cookie camouflage such as `xPaddingObfsMode` with `tokenish` placement and `sessionID`/`seq` moved out of the URL path) reliably avoids triggering automated CDN anti-abuse/throttling, and (2) on a direct VPS (`steal-oneself`, Chrome 155+ fingerprint), do `FinalMask` or `REALITY + XHTTP` offer any practical resilience gain over `REALITY + Vision`?

Following Xue et al. (NDSS '25), long-lived multiplexed connections stand out by flow longevity (>97% of ISP flows) and cross-layer RTT variance. issues.title: Reseed server `coconut.incognet.io` serves SU3 with empty RouterInfo files
issues.body:
When doing some testing today (2026-11-21), I noticed that `https://coconut.incognet.io/i2pseeds.su3` contains 100 zip entries, all of which were zero bytes in length (e.g. `routerInfo-j0eELJO7ndA9c4A95NE-T~F4mXI-3aM4c5gTd0xOy4o=.dat`). The other default reseed servers seemed to be fine.

This results in several "Identity: Buffer length 0 is too small" errors when a new router attempts to reseed from it (so, to be precise, about 100 log entries), which makes it look like a memory problem.

I guess some potential solutions here include removing this reseed server until the issue is fixed, or just skipping entries in `Reseeder::ProcessZIPStream` that decompress to fewer bytes than a minimal identity, with only one log warning shown per bundle to prevent log spam.

Edit: it looks like this server has been publishing faulty bundles since at least last April (seven months at this point). See: #2372

issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [X] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [X] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [X] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [X] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [X] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

**Cause**

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. XDRIVE has no peer liveness signal: no heartbeat, no idle timeout. `Conn.receive` blocks on the reader channel (`conn.go:53-61`), `walReader.poll` returns quietly on an empty listing (`wal.go:295-297`), `holeTimeout` fires only when later segments exist (`wal.go:312-321`), EOF comes only from a `.end` object (`wal.go:365`).
- No backpressure: `walWriter.Write` appends to the buffer and `flushLocked` starts `go w.upload` (`wal.go:73-91`, `wal.go:127-156`); the semaphore in `upload` limits concurrent `Put`s, not unconsumed data (`wal.go:161-166`). Segments are deleted only by the peer's reader, so nothing limits what

TUN inbound: Support a configurable Wintun adapter GUID on Windows (#7458)
issues.body:
Implements #7458.

Adds an optional "guid" to the TUN inbound, used when Xray creates the Wintun adapter:

  "settings": { "name": "xray0", "guid": "6ba7b810-9dad-11d1-80b4-00c04fd430c8" }

- Omitted: the GUID is still MD5 of the name, nothing changes.
- Set: passed to wintun.CreateAdapter. An adapter that already has the name is
  still opened by name and reused, so the name stays the primary key.
- Windows only, but validated as a canonical GUID on every platform, so a typo
  fails at config load instead of at TUN start.
- windows.GUID is built explicitly with the first three groups little-endian,
  which is what the old unsafe reinterpretation of the MD5 bytes produced, so
  the default path is unchanged.

Files: proxy/tun/config.proto (+ regenerated config.pb.go), new proxy/tun/guid.go,
tun_windows.go, infra/conf/tun.go, tests (including a //go:build windows one for
the GUID layout), and a paragraph in proxy/tun/README.md.

Tested: go test ./proxy/tun/ ./infra/conf/, builds for windows/amd64+arm64,
darwin/arm64, freebsd/amd64, linux/arm64, GOOS=windows go vet,
vprotogen -mode check.

issues.title: VLESS: run multiplexing directly on transport
issues.body:
This PR moves Multiplex to `proxy/vless/multiplex` and VLESS Reverse to `proxy/vless/reverse`. VLESS, VMess, and Reverse share the same Multiplex implementation. These paths pass decoded traffic through `DispatchLink` without intermediate `pipe` links.

### Protocol support

**Outbound Multiplex is supported only for VLESS and VMess.** The old generic `mux.cool` is disabled for all other outbound protocols.

VMess uses the shared implementation for both inbound and outbound Mux. Ordinary VMess TCP and UDP keep the direct path from #5143. Reverse uses the VLESS implementation. The old standalone Reverse application has been removed.

### VLESS configuration

Use `outbounds[].settings.multiplex`. An empty object `{}` enables Multiplex with the defaults. The following fragment shows the same settings explicitly:

```json
"multiplex": {
  "enabled": true,
  "concurrency": 8,
  "xudpConcurrency": 0,
  "xudpProxyUDP443": "reject"
}
```

- `enabled`: set to `false` to disable Multiplex. Omit it to enable Multiplex when the object is present.
- `concurrency`: maximum active streams per connection in the shared pool. Omit it or set it to `0` to use `8`. A negative value disables the shared pool. XDrive uses a minimum of `128` when that pool is enabled.
- `xudpConcurrency`: a positive value enables a separate UDP pool and sets its concurrency. `0` uses the shared pool when available. A negative value sends UDP outside Multiplex. The `xudpProxyUDP443` policy is checked first for UDP/443.
- `xudpProxyUDP443`: `reject` is the JSON default and reports `XUDP rejected UDP/443 traffic`. `skip` sends the request through the ordinary outbound path. `allow` permits Multiplex when a suitable pool is available.

The legacy `outbounds[].mux` object with `"enabled": true` still works for VLESS. When both forms are present, `settings.multiplex` takes precedence, including when it explicitly sets `"enabled": false`. Multiplex is disabled when both forms are absent.

### VMess configuration

Use the existing `outbounds[].mux` object alongside `protocol` and `settings`. The `settings.multiplex` field is VLESS-only. This fragment goes in the outbound object:

```json
"mux": {
  "enabled": true,
  "concurrency": 8,
  "xudpConcurrency": 0,
  "xudpProxyUDP443": "reject"
}
```

The same pool and UDP/443 settings apply. Set `"enabled": true` explicitly to enable the legacy `mux` object.

### Other outbound protocols

If `outbounds[].mux.enabled` is set to `true` for another protocol, Xray logs the following warning when loading the configuration or creating the outbound through the API:

`Mux is no longer supported by this outbound protocol; ordinary outbound connections will be used.`

When Xray reads JSON, the warning appears in the command's standard output (`stdout`), including when using `xray api ado`. If an API client submits a pre-built outbound configuration, the running Xray instance writes the warning to its configured log if the log settings allow warnings.

Startup continues and that outbound uses ordinary connections. A disabled `mux` setting does not produce this warning.

issues.title: REALITY: per-SNI target, so SNI routing does not need an external L4 proxy (JARM goes to zeros)
issues.body:
Related: #2374, #5420, #2108.

#2374 asked for this and was answered with "use an L4 proxy". The catch: with nginx/haproxy ssl_preread in front, JARM of the server returns all zeros, which is exactly the server-side fingerprint REALITY exists to avoid. So SNI routing currently costs the property it is supposed to protect.

Proposal: allow a target per serverName, resolved inside REALITY.

"realitySettings": {
  "target": "default.example:443",
  "targets": { "other.example": "other.example:443" },
  "serverNames": ["default.example", "other.example"]
}

Pick the splice target from the received SNI; fall back to `target` when there is no match; keep configs without `targets` unchanged. Also fixes the cert mismatch: today every extra serverName gets the default target's certificate, which is invalid for that name and breaks plain-TLS clients and probes on it (see YouzSpace/3xui-hub#38).

Watch: read the SNI before splicing without an extra round trip; only allow targets present in serverNames; keep record sizes and timings identical.

Also worth documenting: fallbacks are not evaluated on REALITY inbounds (#5420), so `path`-based fallback is not an alternative.

issues.title: TUN inbound: Half-close the app connection when the outbound is done, instead of waiting for `uplinkOnly`
issues.body:
## Why

With Xray's TUN as the system VPN, an app that reads a response until the server closes waits about 1 s more than it should on every such connection. The outbound already knows the response is over, but TUN keeps the app's connection open until the whole dispatch ends, and that happens only after `uplinkOnly`. Examples are HTTP/1.0 without `Content-Length`, RTSP (Moonlight in #5845) and simple request and reply protocols. With this change the app gets the end of the response right away

## What changed

- TUN sends FIN to the app as soon as the outbound is done with the response. The app can still send, and the connection is closed as before when the dispatch is over
- the lightweight TCP stack gets `CloseWrite` for that
- the rest of the core still closes links in pairs, as agreed in the thread

## Testing and limits

- `TestTCPCloseWrite` checks that FIN goes out, that data from the app is still read after it and that `Close` sends nothing more. `go test -race ./proxy/tun` passes
- this helps only when the outbound itself sees the end of the response, for example freedom or VMess. Over VLESS the outbound ends only after `uplinkOnly` on the server, so the wait there stays

Related #5845 #7345

issues.title: grpc: close cached clients with their outbound handler
issues.body:
Related to #7177. Requesting review of resource ownership, shutdown semantics, and API compatibility

## Problem

Outbound gRPC clients are cached by destination and MemoryStreamConfig, but core shutdown never closes or removes them. In an embedding process that stays alive, clients can retain connections and continue reconnecting after their core has stopped.

## Change

Give memory stream settings synchronous close-hook registration, and close the resources from their owning outbound handler. Register each ClientConn for exact-entry cache removal and ClientConn.Close. Refuse both reuse and creation after owner closure starts; racing creation must either register for cleanup or close its unpublished client. Cleanup runs outside the settings/cache locks, and concurrent Close callers wait for the same result.

The supported Instance lifecycle is single-start. Each fresh core retains separate ownership even when endpoint and outbound tags match. No per-run generation model, idle-timeout change or per-RPC closure of the shared ClientConn is added.

## Validation

- Synthetic regression reproduces the problem on v26.3.27 and main da2248c.
- `go test -race ./transport/internet ./transport/internet/grpc -count=1 -timeout=120s` passes on this exact branch.
- Official `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./` passes.
- Tests cover two live cores, sibling streams, normal/MultiMode, fresh-core cycles, failed-start cleanup, multiple destinations, owner/acquisition races, cancellation/backoff and forced dialerProxy lookup contention with Manager.Close.
- Earlier candidate testing also ran the target race suites five times and the dialerProxy test ten times. Those results are supplementary, not a claim that the whole upstream suite passes.

## Review questions / limits

- Handler.Close previously always returned nil. This candidate propagates cleanup errors. Is propagation preferred, or should transport cleanup be logged while preserving the existing return policy? Embedders must distinguish a cleanup error from a still-running core.
- MemoryStreamConfig with resource/mutex state must not be copied; direct external transport callers must close their settings.
- Manager.RemoveHandler still bypasses Handler.Close. XHTTP/nested download settings and TUN eventfd cleanup remain unfixed.
- No general multi-instance guarantee for Xray's other process-global networking state, TLS/Reality/masking matrix, or physical Android packet boundary is claimed.

This is intended as a draft for ownership/API review, not a claim that the Android product defect is resolved.

issues.title: Freedom: Fix PROXY protocol client address encoding across TCP and UDP
issues.body:
**Problem**
When proxyProtocol is set on a Freedom outbound, the PROXY protocol header is built from the inbound source address and the remote address of the outgoing connection. However, `proxyproto.HeaderProxyFromAddrs` only fills in the addresses when the source address and the destination address are of the same type: both TCP or both UDP. If they differ, it falls back to an UNSPEC/UNKNOWN header and leaves the addresses out. The backend then never sees the real client IP. 

This happens whenever the client's transport protocol doesn't match the one Freedom uses to reach the destination. For example:
- The client connects over UDP (QUIC-based inbounds such as Hysteria2, or UDP-based transports) and the request goes out over TCP
- The client connects over TCP and the traffic goes out as UDP

**Solution**
This PR updates proxy header construction to match the source address type to the destination transport when constructing the header. This preserves the client IP and port for both UDP-to-TCP and TCP-to-UDP address conversion. The change is limited to header construction.

**Testing**
- Verified that a TCP listener receives the original IPv4 and IPv6 client endpoints with PROXY v1 and v2.
- Verified that a TCP source and UDP destination produce a PROXY v2 UDP header with the original endpoints.
- Ran the PROXY protocol, finalmask, Freedom, and configuration package tests. All passed.

issues.title: Happy Eyeballs: add successDefinition to race until TLS handshake completes
issues.body:
## Motivation

When the server's domain resolves to several IPs, Happy Eyeballs is supposed to pick a working one. In Russia, however, some ISPs (the DPI boxes installed at them) drop the ServerHello for some of these IPs while TCP to them still connects. Which IPs are affected differs from one ISP and region to another and changes over time: an IP that is blocked for one client works for another, so removing it from DNS would only break it for everyone else. Happy Eyeballs today ends the race at the first TCP connection, so it happily picks such an IP, and then the TLS or REALITY handshake can never complete. A retry usually picks the same IP again, because it wins the TCP race again. In this situation the current Happy Eyeballs is of no use at all, even though other IPs of the same domain work fine.

## What this PR adds

A new optional field `successDefinition` in `sockopt.happyEyeballs`:

| Value | The race is won by |
|---|---|
| `tcpConnected` (default) | the first established TCP connection, as before |
| `tlsHandshakeComplete` | the first connection that completes the TLS or REALITY handshake |

```json
"sockopt": {
  "domainStrategy": "UseIP",
  "happyEyeballs": {
    "tryDelayMs": 250,
    "maxConcurrentTry": 4,
    "successDefinition": "tlsHandshakeComplete"
  }
}
```

Without `successDefinition`, or with `tcpConnected`, nothing changes. Without TLS or REALITY, `tlsHandshakeComplete` is the same as `tcpConnected`.

The behaviour follows section 6.1 of Happy Eyeballs v3, which says clients SHOULD wait for the TLS handshake to complete before canceling other attempts: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-happy-happyeyeballs-v3/
Chromium's Happy Eyeballs v3 implementation does the same: a TCP-based attempt runs the TLS handshake inside it and completes only when the handshake does, and an attempt counts as slow (so the next one starts) if TCP and TLS together take longer than the connection attempt delay:
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/socket/tls_stream_attempt.cc
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/http/http_stream_pool_attempt.cc

Happy Eyeballs v3 is still a draft, and browsers do not use it by default yet: in Chromium it is behind the `HappyEyeballsV3` feature, which is disabled by default, and Firefox enables it only in Nightly.

## How it works

- The scheduler of `TcpRaceDial` is reused as is (`tryDelayMs`, `maxConcurrentTry`, `prioritizeIPv6`, `interleave`); only the attempt it runs differs. With `tcpConnected` the attempt is the same system dial as before.
- With `tlsHandshakeComplete` every attempt goes through TCP dial to one IP → FinalMask (if any) → the transport's own TLS or REALITY handshake. Only the TCP destination changes from attempt to attempt; masks apply to each attempt separately, exactly as on a normal dial.
- An attempt keeps its `maxConcurrentTry` slot until its handshake ends, and a hanging handshake does not stop the scheduler from starting the next attempt after `tryDelayMs`.
- Losing attempts are stopped by closing their connections. Transports that leave the handshake to the first write (gRPC, and HTTPUpgrade and XHTTP with Go TLS) get it completed inside the race, so a connection is never handshaked twice.
- The race happens under the same conditions as the TCP race in `DialSystem`: `domainStrategy` set, at least two IPs, no `dialerProxy`, non-zero `tryDelayMs` and `maxConcurrentTry`. Otherwise the transport dials exactly as before.

All covered transports now dial through `internet.DialTCPWithHandshake(ctx, dest, streamSettings, handshake)`. `handshake` is a function that wraps the TCP connection with the transport's TLS or REALITY client; it holds the same code the transport used to run right after its own TCP dial.

Transports covered: RAW (TLS, REALITY), WebSocket, HTTPUpgrade, gRPC (TLS, REALITY), XHTTP over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (TLS, REALITY), MASQUE over HTTP/2. For XHTTP the race runs once per new physical connection. UDP

WebSocket transport: Stop the heartbeat goroutine on Close
issues.body:
## Why

With `heartbeatPeriod` set, every WebSocket connection starts a goroutine that sleeps for the period and sends a ping. It only exits when a ping fails to write, and `Close()` does not wake it, so a closed connection stays in memory with its gorilla buffers until the next ping is due. With short connections and a period of tens of seconds these pile up.

## What changed

The ping goroutine now waits on a ticker and on a `done.Instance` that `Close()` closes, so the goroutine exits right away. The ping itself and its period stay the same.

## Testing and limits

`TestCloseStopsHeartbeat` closes a connection with a one hour period and checks that the goroutine count goes back to where it was before the dial. It fails on `main`, where the goroutine sleeps for the whole hour.

Measured on a build based on v26.10.31, on a CDN emulator with 100 short connections and three bursts of 24, ping every 45 s.

| | goroutines at the end | memory at the end |
| -- | -- | -- |
| no heartbeat | 27 | 40.8 MB |
| heartbeat, before | 104 | 45.2 MB |
| heartbeat, this PR | 21 | 38.3 MB |

With the change the ping still keeps idle connections of 70 and 120 s alive through an emulator that drops them after 60 s without data.

`go test -race ./transport/internet/websocket/` passes.

issues.title: XMC config: split role-specific settings into `clients`/`servers` blocks / XMC 配置：按角色拆分 `clients`/`servers` 区块
issues.body:
### Summary / 概要

XMC's `settings` currently mixes both ends of a connection in one flat object:

- `hostname` is only used by the dialing side.
- `yggdrasil` means "log in with these credentials" on the client and "verify players through this API" on the server, yet both live in the same object.
- `paddings` is a single timeline where every turn repeats `direction: "c2s" | "s2c"`.
- `noPadding` and an explicit empty `paddings: []` are two ways to express the same thing.

This proposal splits the role-specific settings into `clients` and `servers` blocks, in the spirit of `header-custom`'s `clients`/`servers` sequences, and keeps every existing field working as a legacy form.

XMC 目前的 `settings` 把一条连接的两端混在同一个扁平对象里：

- `hostname` 只有拨号侧（客户端）使用；
- `yggdrasil` 在客户端是“用这组账号登录”，在服务端是“通过这个 API 校验玩家”，却放在同一个对象里；
- `paddings` 是一条共享时间线，每轮都要重复写 `direction: "c2s" | "s2c"`；
- `noPadding` 和显式空数组 `paddings: []` 表达的是同一件事，有两条关闭路径。

本提案把角色相关的配置拆到 `clients` / `servers` 两个区块（参考 `header-custom` 的 `clients`/`servers` 序列），并保留所有旧字段作为兼容形式。

Context: this is a config-only follow-up to the XMC padding work (#6769, #7402) and Yggdrasil login (#7416). It does not touch the Minecraft wire protocol or the runtime behavior.

背景：这是 XMC padding（#6769、#7402）与 Yggdrasil 登录（#7416）之后的纯配置整理，不改 Minecraft 线协议，也不改运行时行为。

### Current config / 现状

```jsonc
{
  "type": "xmc",
  "settings": {
    "hostname": "mc.example.com",
    "password": "shared-secret",
    "profiles": [ /* ... */ ],
    "yggdrasil": { "api": "https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil", "username": "u", "password": "p", "player": "Player" },
    "paddings": [
      { "length": "2",     "direction": "c2s", "delay": "5" },
      { "length": "47-72", "direction": "s2c", "delay": "0-20" },
      { "length": "37-51", "direction": "c2s", "delay": "2-22" }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Proposed config / 新配置

```jsonc
{
  "type": "xmc",
  "settings": {
    // Shared by both sides / 两端共享
    "password": "shared-secret",
    "profiles": [ /* ... */ ],

    "clients": {
      "hostname": "mc.example.com",
      "yggdrasil": { "api": "https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil", "username": "u", "password": "p", "player": "Player" },
      "paddings": [
        { "length": "2",     "delay": "5" },
        { "length": "37-51", "delay": "2-22" }
      ]
    },

    "servers": {
      "yggdrasil": { "api": "https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil" },
      "paddings": [
        { "length": "47-72", "delay": "0-20" }
      ]
    },

    "noPadding": false
  }
}
```

### Merge semantics / 合并语义

`clients.paddings[i]` and `servers.paddings[i]` form one round: the client turn is sent first, then the server turn. When the lists differ in length, the leftover turns of the longer list are appended. This reproduces the built-in 26.1.2 preset exactly, because that preset is a strictly alternating c2s/s2c timeline.

The two lists must be given together, because each side needs the peer's per-turn `delay` minimum to stay in phase. `direction` is implied by the block and must be left unset inside `clients`/`servers`. A configured list is the complete schedule and still replaces the preset entirely, including the preset's Play-state join tail.

`clients.paddings[i]` 与 `servers.paddings[i]` 组成一轮：先客户端轮、再服务端轮；两侧长度不同时，较长一侧多出的轮次追加在末尾。内置 26.1.2 preset 正好是严格 c2s/s2c 交替，因此可以无损拆成两份。

两份列表必须成对出现：每一侧都需要对端每轮的 `delay` 最小值才能对齐时间线。方向由所在区块决定，`clients`/`servers` 内不允许再写 `direction`。配置后的列表仍是完整时间线，会整体替换 preset（含 preset 的 Play join 尾巴）。

### Compatibility / 兼容性

No wire-format or runtime change: the new form is parsed into the same merged timeline the runtime already uses (`xmc.Config.Paddings`). The runtime proto is intentionally unchanged in the draft PR; the split is a JSON-level migration.

Legacy fields keep working exactly as before: `hostname`, `password`, `profiles`, `paddings` (with `direction`), `yggdrasil`, `noPadding`. Mixing the legacy and split forms of the same setting is rejected with a clear error.

issues.body:
重写 Lua 文档的时候被迫写了下面加粗的这段，觉得十分不科学，应该把它做成和 targetStrategy 一样防环，没有大的副作用。各出站的行为也比较统一。

> ::: warning 循环依赖
任意查询交给内置 DNS 模块处理时，若选中 DNS 服务器的 `address` 不含 `+local`，则到该服务器的连接会交给路由。若 `address` 是域名，路由脚本可能再次调用内置 DNS 解析它。新的查询可能按 DNS 和路由规则顺利完成，也可能经过多个 DNS 服务器和出站，重新依赖尚未完成的解析，形成死循环。

> 为避免这种潜在的循环依赖，DNS 模块会将自身发起的所有连接标记为 `skipDNSResolve = true`。核心原生的路由模块不检查是否真的成环，而是据此标记简单粗暴地跳过 DNS 解析，直接杜绝成环可能；请求随后继续匹配其余规则并交给出站。Lua 脚本需要自行处理该标记，建议同样跳过解析，也可以按需扩展处理方式。

> **Freedom 出站不会检查 `skipDNSResolve`。若脚本将这类连接交给它，且其 `sockopt.domainStrategy` 非 `AsIs`，就会再次调用内置 DNS 解析该域名。路由脚本无法干预出站的解析，需另行规避，不再赘述；其他出站的 `targetStrategy` 会像路由一样检查该标记跳过解析以避免成环。**

> 其他出站也有另一种成环路径。若代理出站的服务器地址为域名，且 `sockopt.domainStrategy` 非 `AsIs`，出站就会调用内置 DNS 解析该地址。例如，出站 A 依赖 DNS A 的解析结果，而 DNS A 的查询又被送回出站 A，就会形成死循环；也可能先送到出站 B，再因解析 B 的服务器地址而回到 DNS A，形成更长的依赖链。这些出站与 DNS 之间的循环与路由脚本无关，需另行规避，此处不再赘述。

issues.title: Finalmask fragment: Add disorder and disoob modes
issues.body:
## Motivation

Russian TSPU has evolved from simple SNI-based blocking to analyzing TCP-level handshake patterns, including shaping and dropping connections based on ClientHello analysis (#5332, #6293). Plain fragmentation alone no longer suffices.

### What TSPU does now

The inspector no longer just reads the first ClientHello record in isolation. It reassembles the client hello **from multiple TCP fragments**, so merely cutting the hello into pieces with delays (the current `fragment` behavior) is not enough: the censor waits for the neighboring segments, collects them into a complete picture, and still sees the SNI. Reports from the issues:

- #5332 "TCP + Reality gets blocked" (148 comments, RPRX participated): "russian censor blocking strategy has evolved significantly... now they've learned to detect anomalies in tcp connection patterns even when the tls handshake completes successfully". The problem lives at the packet/flow level, not just at SNI level.
- #6293 "Russia blocks 2026": users report that nothing else helped - fragmentation, mux, SNI change, even the host - i.e. the existing `fragment` mask alone is no longer sufficient against current TSPU behavior. Also noted: Roskomnadzor has been matching known TLS fingerprint lists, so plain fragment needs a next-level countermeasure.
- RPRX closing #5332 with a promise to keep finding ways around censorship ("as long as the network is not completely cut off, we will find a way out") - this feature is exactly in line with the project's stated goals.
- The sqsvp comment in #6293 observes that TSPU sits in front of the NAT, which is precisely the hop the disorder trick exploits (see below).

Prior art: byedpi (hufrea/byedpi) `--disorder` / `--disoob` modes, zapret and GoodbyeDPI, all of which converged on the same class of TCP-level tricks against the Russian censor. Only the concept is reused here, no code.

### How disorder defeats reassembly

The ClientHello is split into segments. Segments with odd index are sent with `TTL=1`:

- They die on the first router hop, which is at or before the TSPU box. The DPI **does see them**, but they never reach the server.
- The server is missing those bytes, so TCP retransmits them via RTO - already with the restored default TTL, and they arrive.
- The censor sees a garbled sequence: half the hello right away, holes, then slow retransmissions. By the time it can reassemble anything reliably, the classification window has passed. Blocking has nothing to latch onto.

`disoob` additionally sends the first segment's boundary byte as TCP urgent data (`MSG_OOB`) with a fake marker value; the real byte follows in the normal stream. DPI implementations that mishandle urgent data choke on it, while ordinary receivers skip the urgent byte and see the byte-exact stream.

This extends the existing finalmask `fragment` mask with a `mode` field: `normal` (default, current behavior byte-for-byte compatible), `disorder`, `disoob`. No new config knobs: TTL is fixed at 1, the urgent marker is fixed. Extending finalmask masks incrementally matches the maintainer's stated intent.

- `transport/internet/finalmask/fragment/config.proto`: `enum Mode { NORMAL, DISORDER, DISOOB }`, field `mode = 13`; `config.pb.go` regenerated with `go run ./infra/vprotogen` (`-mode check` passes).
- `transport/internet/finalmask/fragment/conn.go`: `Write()` refactored into split (`splitClientHello`/`splitRaw`) + send (`writeSegments`) phases, so segments can be flagged before any byte goes out. `markDisorder` flags odd-index segments. issues.title: REALITY client: Drop the handshake state once the handshake is done
issues.body:
## Why

A REALITY client connection keeps everything its ClientHello was built from until it closes, the ML-KEM-768 key of the key share among it. That is about 12 KiB per connection, 8 KiB of it the key, and none of it is used again. With VLESS every TCP connection of an app and every UDP flow without XUDP has its own connection to the server, so on a phone there are hundreds of copies at once.

## What changed

After a successful `HandshakeContext`, `UClient` resets `uConn.HandshakeState` and `uConn.Extensions`. Nothing on the wire changes and the fingerprint stays the same. In uTLS these fields are only read while the handshake runs, `Read`, `Write`, KeyUpdate and NewSessionTicket handling do not touch them, and the REALITY code that reads them (`VerifyPeerCertificate`, the `show` output) runs inside the handshake.

## Testing and limits

Measured on a build based on v26.10.31, on a local stand with 300 sessions through VLESS + REALITY, memory of xray per live session.

| session | before | this PR |
| -- | -- | -- |
| TCP | 89.4 KB | 77.4 KB |
| UDP | 111.0 KB | 96.2 KB |

In a heap profile before the change the ML-KEM keys (`NewDecapsulationKey768`) hold 2.5 MB for 300 sessions.

`TestVlessXtlsVisionReality`, `TestVlessRealityFingerprints` and `TestVlessXtlsVision` pass. Connections on the stand lived for seconds, so a long connection that gets a KeyUpdate was not run.

The plain TLS client with a uTLS fingerprint keeps the same state, this PR leaves it alone.

issues.body:
A peer that accepts TCP and stalls during TLS/REALITY negotiation can retain an outbound operation while the dispatch context remains alive. In the reported burstObservatory setup, descriptor growth accompanied memory pressure and intermittent loss of connectivity on a Keenetic Giga (KN-1012) EAEU with 512 MB RAM.

The timeout begins after TCP establishment. Eight seconds is the value used for the local mitigation and proposed here for review. Slow handshakes exceeding that duration will fail. TCP establishment retains its existing independent timeout.

Hysteria, MASQUE, XDRIVE & XHTTP/3 clients: Close the packet conn before the QUIC transport
issues.body:
When a client dials through `sockopt.dialerProxy`, its packet conn is a `FakePacketConn` over `cnc.Connection`, and `SetReadDeadline` on it does nothing. `quic.Transport.Close()` stops its read loop only through that deadline and then waits for the loop to return, so closing the transport before the packet conn blocks until the tunnel under it closes by itself.

In the Hysteria client this happens in `client.close()` with the client lock held, so every new dial on that outbound waits. I hit it with a Hysteria outbound behind another Hysteria outbound and an apernet Hysteria 2.14.0 server at the end (default `maxIdleTimeout` of 30s). After 35 seconds of idle the next request timed out, and the outbound stayed dead for about two minutes. With a request every 60 seconds it never recovered.

Fix: close the packet conn first, then the transport, as #7413 did for one XHTTP/3 path. This covers the Hysteria client and the same calls in MASQUE, XDRIVE and the XHTTP/3 `context.AfterFunc`. With the fix, the Hysteria setup above reconnects on the first request after idle: 0 failures in 36 requests, against two-minute stalls before.

issues.title: XTLS Vision: Track TLS record boundaries across writes
issues.body:
Fixes https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/7164

`IsCompleteRecord` checks each write on its own, so once a write ends inside a record, no later write can pass. With back-to-back records Vision then pads the whole transfer. This is a smaller take on the idea in #7307: one function replaces `IsCompleteRecord`, and the diff is +53 −51 in `proxy/proxy.go` plus a test file.

`VisionWriter` keeps two fields: how many bytes of the current record are still to come, and the record's type. `tlsRecordEnd` walks the record headers in each write from that point. It returns the end of the last complete application data record (0 if the write holds a handshake record). The padding ends exactly there with `CommandPaddingDirect`, as #5179 requires. The rest of the write is written right after the switch, through the existing direct-copy path. If the stream is not TLS records, or a write ends inside a record header, tracking is lost. Each write is then checked from its first byte, as before.

The receiver and the wire format are unchanged, so old and new versions work together in both directions.

**Repro from #7164** (tlsblast, 1 GB, back-to-back 16 KiB records, VLESS + TLS + Vision over 127.0.0.1, `loglevel: warning`, macOS arm64, 3 runs; CPU is client + server seconds):

| 1 GB | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| upload | 3.1 Gbit/s, 2.0 + 3.6 s CPU | 12–15 Gbit/s, 0.5 + 0.6 s CPU |
| download | 2.4–3.4 Gbit/s, 3.4 + 1.8 s CPU | 11–16 Gbit/s, 0.6 + 0.6 s CPU |

At `loglevel: debug`, with 64 MiB per transfer:
- main: 16,408 `XtlsPadding` lines on the sender.
- This PR, upload: the client switches on its first write, ending the padding right after ChangeCipherSpec + Finished (`XtlsPadding 64 … 2`).
- This PR, download: the server ends the padding at the end of the first full application data record (`XtlsPadding 22 … 2`, 16,406 bytes in). It does not switch in the write that holds the handshake flight.
- All four main/PR client/server pairs complete. The speedup follows the patched sender's direction.

**Tests**
- New `proxy/vision_test.go`. It covers upload and download streams, cut by various batch sizes, and checks:
  - the padding ends with `CommandPaddingDirect` at the expected record boundary;
  - the padded part plus the raw part equals the original stream.

  It also has table cases for `tlsRecordEnd`. The writer test fails on main.
- `go test -race ./proxy/ ./proxy/vless/... ./proxy/freedom/... ./common/buf/...` passes.
- `go test ./testing/scenarios -run TestVless` passes, including `TestVlessXtlsVision` and `TestVlessXtlsVisionReality`.

---

中文简述：`IsCompleteRecord` 按单次写入判断，记录一旦跨写入就再也无法通过，背靠背的大记录会导致整个连接一直 padding。本 PR 在 `VisionWriter` 里记录当前 TLS 记录剩余的字节数和记录类型，在每次写入中找到最后一个完整 application data 记录的结尾：padding 恰好在记录边界结束（保持 #5179 的保证），剩余部分在切换后直接写出。不含握手记录的写入才会切换。接收端与协议格式不变，新旧版本互通。比 #7307 简单很多，只替换了一个函数。

issues.title: Feature Request: Support a configurable Wintun adapter GUID on Windows
issues.body:
Currently, Xray-core derives the Wintun adapter GUID from the configured interface name using MD5:

id := md5.Sum([]byte(name))
guid := (*windows.GUID)(unsafe.Pointer(&id[0]))

This provides deterministic adapter identity based on the interface name, which works well for standard use cases.

However, there are scenarios where applications need to control the Wintun adapter identity independently of its display name.

I propose adding an optional "guid" field to the TUN inbound configuration, allowing users to specify a fixed Wintun adapter GUID on Windows.

Proposed Configuration

{
  "protocol": "tun",
  "settings": {
    "name": "xray0",
    "guid": "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx",
    "mtu": 1500
  }
}

The "guid" field would be optional.

- If specified, Xray-core uses the provided GUID when opening or creating the Wintun adapter.
- If omitted, Xray-core retains the existing behavior of deriving the GUID from the interface name using MD5.
- On non-Windows platforms, the field is ignored.

Motivation

A configurable GUID would be useful for applications managing multiple network engines, configurations, or profiles that need to coordinate access to a consistent Wintun adapter identity.

For example:

- Multiple engine instances sharing a common TUN device identity.
- Applications that need to identify an adapter independently of its display name.
- Maintaining adapter identity across interface renames or configuration changes.
- Integrations where the host application manages adapter lifecycle and needs predictable adapter identification.

Windows adapter identity and interface naming are separate concerns. Allowing an explicit GUID would provide additional flexibility without changing the default behavior.

Proposed Implementation

1. Add an optional "guid" string field to the TUN configuration in "infra/conf/tun.go".
2. Add the corresponding field to "proxy/tun/config.proto".
3. Regenerate the protobuf bindings.
4. Pass the GUID through "TunOptions".
5. Update the Windows implementation to use the provided GUID when present.
6. Preserve the existing MD5-based GUID generation as the fallback.
7. Accept and ignore the field on non-Windows platforms.

Backward Compatibility

This change would be fully backward-compatible.

Existing configurations would continue using the current MD5-based GUID derivation, with no changes to existing behavior.

Platform Support

This option would only have an effect on Windows, where Wintun adapter creation and identification use GUIDs.

Other platforms would ignore the option.

Additional Considerations

The supplied GUID should be validated as a canonical UUID.

Users should ensure that explicitly configured GUIDs do not conflict with GUIDs assigned to unrelated Wintun adapters.

The default behavior should remain unchanged to avoid breaking existing configurations.

Question

Would maintainers consider adding an optional, Windows-specific "guid" configuration field to the TUN inbound?

I would be happy to contribute an implementation if this feature is considered appropriate.

issues.title: XMC finalmask: Split config into clients/servers blocks
issues.body:
Refs #7455. Draft: this PR only makes the proposal concrete; the design is waiting for discussion in the issue and should not be merged as-is.

## What / 做了什么

Split the XMC JSON settings by role, in the spirit of `header-custom`'s `clients`/`servers` sequences:

- `clients` holds the client-only `hostname`, the Yggdrasil login credentials, and the client-to-server padding turns.
- `servers` holds the Yggdrasil verification endpoint and the server-to-client padding turns.
- `password` and `profiles` stay shared at the top level.
- Padding turns inside a role block no longer carry `direction`; the block selects the sender.

参考 `header-custom` 的 `clients`/`servers`，把 XMC 的 JSON 配置按角色拆分：

- `clients`：客户端专属的 `hostname`、Yggdrasil 登录账号、c2s padding 轮次；
- `servers`：Yggdrasil 校验 API、s2c padding 轮次；
- `password` / `profiles` 保持在顶层共享；
- 角色区块内的 padding 轮次不再写 `direction`，由所在区块决定方向。

```jsonc
"settings": {
  "password": "shared-secret",
  "profiles": [ /* ... */ ],

  "clients": {
    "hostname": "mc.example.com",
    "yggdrasil": { "api": "https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil", "username": "u", "password": "p" },
    "paddings": [ { "length": "2", "delay": "5" }, { "length": "37-51", "delay": "2-22" } ]
  },

  "servers": {
    "yggdrasil": { "api": "https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil" },
    "paddings": [ { "length": "47-72", "delay": "0-20" } ]
  }
}
```

## Semantics / 语义

`clients.paddings[i]` and `servers.paddings[i]` form one round (`c2s` then `s2c`); the leftover turns of the longer list are appended. The two lists must be given together, because each side needs the peer's per-turn `delay` minimum to stay in phase. A configured list is still the complete schedule and replaces the preset entirely.

issues.title: Fix WireGuard domain routing by restoring context tags and adding thread safety
Fix multi-peer WireGuard with unified reader architecture
issues.body:
When WireGuard outbound is configured with multiple peers, only one peer could be active at a time. Attempting to use a second peer would cause handshake failures and connection timeouts.

## Root Cause

The original implementation had each peer connection spawn a reader goroutine that competed for read requests from a shared `readQueue`. When a goroutine grabbed a request but its connection had no data, it would block indefinitely on `c.Read()`, preventing other peer connections from receiving packets. This caused the symptom where only the first connected peer would work, and attempting to use a second peer would break both peers.

Additionally, the `netBindClient` was storing the context from the first connection request and reusing it for all subsequent peer connections, which could cause context cancellation issues.

## Changes

**Unified reader architecture:**
- **Eliminated blocking**: Each peer connection now continuously reads from its socket into a shared data channel
- **Single dispatcher**: A unified `unifiedReader()` goroutine coordinates between incoming data and WireGuard's read requests
- **No race conditions**: All peer connections are monitored simultaneously without competing for requests
- **Scalable**: Works with any number of peers without blocking or starvation

**Fixed context handling:**
- Changed the bind to use `core.ToBackgroundDetachedContext(ctx)` to prevent context cancellation issues
- Ensures peer connections remain independent and stable

**Robustness improvements:**
- Added bounds checking to prevent panics
- Used `sync.Once` to prevent double-close panics
- Named constants for buffer sizes
- Proper cleanup on shutdown

## Solution

### Before:
- Each peer's reader goroutine competed for read requests
- Readers blocked indefinitely waiting for data on their connections
- Only one peer could work at a time; switching peers broke both

### After:
- Each peer continuously reads and sends data to a shared channel
- Single dispatcher matches received data with read requests
- All peer connections work simultaneously without blocking
- Clean separation between connection reading and request dispatching

## Testing

- ✅ WireGuard unit tests pass
- ✅ Code review completed
- ✅ Security scan (CodeQL) - no vulnerabilities
- ✅ Robust error handling and edge case coverage

issues.title: Fix occasional SSL protocol error in XTLS Vision direct copy mode
issues.body:
Fixes occasional `ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR` / `ERR_SSL_BAD_RECORD_MAC_ALERT` when using VLESS + XTLS Vision + Reality. The issue is more frequent with `testpre` (pre-connect) enabled.

## Root Cause

When Vision switches to direct copy mode (bypassing outer TLS for splice), it was merging `rawInput` bytes into the output buffer. The `rawInput` buffer in Go's `crypto/tls.Conn` may contain **encrypted** bytes for partial TLS records not yet processed, corrupting the data stream.

## Changes

- **Removed `rawInput` merging**: Only merge `input` (decrypted application data) into the buffer
- **Defer switch when `rawInput` has pending data**: If `rawInput` is not empty, return early and retry on next read cycle, allowing the TLS layer to process remaining encrypted bytes
- **Fix fast-path condition**: Add `w.input == nil` check to ensure fast-path only triggers after switch is complete

```go
// Before: merged encrypted rawInput bytes (incorrect)
if rawInputBuffer, err := buf.ReadFrom(w.rawInput); err == nil && !rawInputBuffer.IsEmpty() {
    buffer, _ = buf.MergeMulti(buffer, rawInputBuffer)
}

// After: defer switch if rawInput has pending encrypted data
if w.rawInput != nil && w.rawInput.Len() > 0 {
    return buffer, err  // retry on next ReadMultiBuffer call
}
```

issues.title: Fix WireGuard inbound domain-based routing
issues.body:
WireGuard inbound sniffing/routing broken since PR #4030. The `sniffingRequest` and `tag` were stored in a shared `routingInfo` struct during `Process()`, causing race conditions when multiple peers connect concurrently—each call overwrites the session info used by `forwardConnection()`.

## Changes

- **Store config at init time**: Extract `tag` and `sniffingRequest` from context in `NewServer()` (same pattern as TUN handler)
- **Simplify `routingInfo`**: Remove `inboundTag`/`contentTag` fields, keep only `ctx` and `dispatcher`
- **Use saved values per-connection**: `forwardConnection()` creates fresh `session.Inbound` and `session.Content` using stored config

```go
// Before: stored during Process(), shared across connections
s.info = routingInfo{
    inboundTag: session.InboundFromContext(ctx),
    contentTag: session.ContentFromContext(ctx),
}

// After: stored during NewServer(), immutable
if inbound := session.InboundFromContext(ctx); inbound != nil {
    server.tag = inbound.Tag
}
if content := session.ContentFromContext(ctx); content != nil {
    server.sniffingRequest = content.SniffingRequest
}
```

tun: add lightweight "system" TCP/IP stack as an alternative to gVisor
issues.body:
gVisor's `stack.Stack` is a general-purpose TCP/IP implementation built for a lossy, reordering public network (congestion control, SACK/RACK, retransmission timers, extra copies). TUN traffic instead flows over a local kernel↔userspace channel that neither drops nor reorders packets, so that generality is pure overhead. This adds an optional, purpose-built stack for TUN that drops the unneeded machinery in exchange for less complexity and fewer copies.

## Backend selection
- New `stack` config option (`proxy/tun/config.proto`, `infra/conf/tun.go`): `"gvisor"` (default, unchanged behavior) or `"system"` (new).
- `proxy/tun/stack.go`: `NewStack()` dispatches on `StackOptions.Backend`; `stack_gvisor.go` is otherwise untouched (renamed constructor only).

## New "system" stack (`proxy/tun/stack_system.go`, `stack_system_tcp.go`)
- Reads/parses IPv4/IPv6 directly off the tun device via the existing `GVisorDevice` interface (now also implemented for this path in `tun_linux.go`/`tun_android.go`), bypassing gVisor's NIC/routing/`stack.Stack` layer entirely.
- UDP and ICMP echo reuse the existing `udpConnectionHandler`/`tun/icmp` handlers as-is — that code was already backend-agnostic.
- TCP gets a small dedicated state machine instead of gVisor's endpoint:
  - In-order-only segment acceptance (no reassembly/SACK); out-of-order or unacceptable segments are dropped and re-acked.
  - Single unified RTO timer covering retransmission, zero-window probing, and lone-FIN resend.
  - Graceful close with a short bounded linger in place of full RFC793 TIME_WAIT.
  - No RST bookkeeping on abort: once a connection is dropped from the table, any stray follow-up packet is naturally answered with a raw RST by the "unknown connection" path.
  - No window scaling/congestion control — advertised window capped at 65535, buffers sized to match gVisor's existing defaults (1 MiB) for comparable throughput on the effectively zero-RTT tun hop.
- Deliberately exposes only plain `net.Conn` `Read`/`Write` (never `ReadMultiBuffer`/`WriteMultiBuffer`) so `stat.CounterConnection`'s byte accounting in `handler.go` isn't silently bypassed.

## Tests
- `proxy/tun/stack_system_test.go` exercises the new stack against a fake in-memory `GVisorDevice`: full handshake + bidirectional echo + graceful close, retransmission on a dropped segment, and idle-connection reaping.

## Example
```json
{
  "inbounds": [{
    "protocol": "tun",
    "settings": {
      "stack": "system"
    }
  }]
}
```

issues.title: xdrive: port latency/throughput optimizations from the reference fork (WAL reader pipelining, slot ring tuning)
issues.body:
移植参考 fork（Ahmad-2213/Xray-core）中 #7208 讨论的优化，降低 XDRIVE 延迟、提升吞吐。重点是使用 slot ring 的 Google Drive。fork 与 main 差异较大，只移植能套进现有结构的部分。

**WAL 路径（`wal.go`）**
- **流水线读取：** `walReader.poll` 保持最多 `concurrency` 个 `Get` 同时进行，队首段按序交付后立即补位，不再等整批完成。
- **写端渐进分段：** `walWriter` 以 `min(segmentBytes, driveInlineLimit)` 起步，连续 `inlineRampSegments` 个满段后翻倍，直到 `segmentBytes`。

**Slot ring 路径（`slots.go`）**
- **默认值：** `slotDepthLimit` 8→16，`slotFetchAhead` 6→10，`slotHuntCeiling` 200ms→100ms，`slotAckRetry` 100ms→30ms，`slotWatermarkTTL` 250ms→100ms。代价是 Drive API 调用和配额消耗增加。
- **提前切到完整段：** 环占用超过 3/4 且缓冲区已有一个完整段时，`size` 直接跳到 `segmentBytes`。
- **忙时合并：** `readyToFlush` 在有 slot 在途时，把小于 `size/2` 的缓冲最多再等 `maxCoalescedTicks` 个周期。
- **卡死超时修正：** `await` 的 `slotStallTimeout` 从「等待开始」和「上次 watermark 进展」中较近的一个算起，慢但存活的读端不会被误判。
- **写重试：** slot 写失败最多重试 `slotWriteAttempts`（3）次，间隔 200ms×n；每次重试前先读该 slot，确认上次写入是否已落地。全部失败才 `fail` 并写错误帧。
- **队首对冲读：** 队首 slot 描述读取超过 `slotHedgeTick`（250ms）未返回时再发一次，总预算 `slotHedgeBudget`（1s），取最先成功的。非队首不对冲。
- **V2 帧：** 帧魔数为 `XDRVSL02`，带 body 的 CRC32，解码和 media body 都会校验。只支持 V2，不再读取 `XDRVSL01`，新旧版本不互连。

**未移植**
- WAL 读端的 probe / 前瞻轮询（以及上传节奏控制、读端瞬时错误容忍）。

**Review 说明**
- 没有跑真实 Google Drive 的 live 测试。时间常量取自参考实现，需要用真实账号验证，尤其是更短的轮询间隔和对冲读是否触发限流。
- `go test -race` 和 gofumpt 格式检查通过。

issues.title: [Feature] XMC: Yggdrasil third-party login + texture signature verification / XMC 支持 Yggdrasil 第三方登录与材质签名验证
issues.body:
> Status: proposal / ready for discussion. Branch: `feat/xmc-yggdrasil-login` (based on `c4561418`), commits `109e8d2c` + `74eb4feb`.
> 状态：提案，欢迎讨论。分支：`feat/xmc-yggdrasil-login`（基于 `c4561418`），提交 `109e8d2c` + `74eb4feb`。

---

## 中文

### 背景与动机

当前 XMC 的登录认证是自造的：

- 客户端配置里手工填写 `username` / `uuid` / `texturesValue` / `texturesSignature`（需要自己去 Mojang 或皮肤站查 UUID、拉签名材质再复制进配置）；
- 服务端用预共享 `password`（同时作为 RSA 私钥的派生种子）加静态 `profiles` 白名单校验；
- Verify Token 尾部追加预共享密码，和 Minecraft 协议本身没有关系。

维护成本高，且无法复用 Minecraft 生态已有的标准在线模式认证（Yggdrasil / authlib-injector / Blessing Skin）。更重要的是，**如果后续要给 MC 模组实现 XMC 服务端**（让真实 MC 客户端或服务端模组走标准 Yggdrasil 登录接入 XMC），预共享密码模型无法对接，因为模组侧只会实现标准的 `authenticate` / `join` / `hasJoined` 流程。

本次改动把 XMC 改成标准 Yggdrasil 登录客户端 + 标准 `hasJoined` 服务端校验，并补上材质签名验证，为后续 MC 模组实现 XMC 服务端铺路，也为 XMC 客户端将来接入真实 MC 服务端打基础。

### 修改内容

涉及文件：

- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/yggdrasil.go`（新增：Yggdrasil HTTP 客户端、登录/刷新/join/hasJoined、验签）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/client.go`（Yggdrasil 登录、标准 hash、材质验签接入）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/server.go`（hasJoined 校验、随机密钥、断连语义）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/profile.go`（多 properties 读写、身份/材质比较）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/config.go`、`config.proto`、`config.pb.go`
- `infra/conf/transport_finalmask.go`（`yggdrasil` 配置解析、随机密钥生成、警告输出）
- 测试：`yggdrasil_test.go`、`profile_test.go`、`handshake_test.go`、`infra/conf/transport_finalmask_xmc_test.go`

#### 1. 配置

XMC `settings` 新增可选的 `yggdrasil` 段：

```json
{
  "type": "xmc",
  "settings": {
    "hostname": "mc.example.com",
    "yggdrasil": {
      "api": "https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil",
      "username": "user@example.com",
      "password": "<skin account password>",
      "player": "Steve"
    }
  }
}
```

- `api`：Yggdrasil API root（例如 Blessing Skin 的 `/api/yggdrasil`）；
- `username` / `password`：客户端登录凭据（邮箱或角色名，取决于 API 实现）；
- `player`：可选；账号有多个角色时必须指定；
- 服务端只需要 `api`，不需要账号密码。

Yggdrasil 模式下顶层 `password` 不再参与握手和密钥派生；旧配置（无 `yggdrasil` 段）行为完全不变。

#### 2. 客户端（client.go / yggdrasil.go）

- 通过 `authserver/authenticate` 登录，多角色时用 `authserver/refresh` 携带 `selectedProfile` 绑定 token；token/clientToken 进程内缓存，`/join` 遇到 403 自动重新登录重试一次。
- Login Start 使用皮肤站返回的真实角色名和 UUID。
- 加密协商完成后按原版算法计算 login hash：

  `sha1(serverId + sharedSecret + serverPublicKey)`，并按 Java `BigInteger#toString(16)` 的二进制补码规则渲染（包含负号和去前导零）。

- **使用 Encryption Request 中实际收到的公钥计算哈希，不再固定配置公钥**；Yggdrasil 模式客户端不需要也不应该去“确认公钥”。
- 用 `accessToken` 真实调用 `sessionserver/session/minecraft/join`。
- 解析 Login Success 的多个 properties，并用 API root 中的 `signaturePublickey` 校验 `textures` 属性签名：
  - SHA1withRSA（与 Blessing Skin 的 `openssl_sign` 默认算法、Minecraft 客户端的签名校验一致）；
  - 支持 PEM / 裸 base64 公钥；
  - 公钥按账号缓存，验签失败时自动重新拉取一次（覆盖皮肤站轮换密钥）；
  - `textures` 缺失、无签名、签名不匹配都会拒绝登录；
  - 校验发生在发送 Login Acknowledged 之前，失败不会进入 play 阶段。
- Yggdrasil 模式不再往 Verify Token 尾部追加预共享密码，保持和原版客户端一致的报文形状。

#### 3. 服务端（server.go）

- Yggdrasil 模式下每个进程随机生成 1024-bit RSA 密钥对（与原版服务端行为一致），**不再从 password 派生**；
- 解密共享密钥后，用自己实际持有的公钥计算同一个 login hash，真实调用 `sessionserver/session/minecraft/hasJoined`；
- 因为客户端 `/join` 与服务端 `/hasJoined` 存在天然竞态，服务端以 200ms 间隔轮询，最长 10s；
- 校验返回的角色 UUID / 名称必须与 Login Start 一致；
- Login Success 直接使用 `hasJoined` 返回的已签名 properties（含 `textures`、`uploadableTextures`）；
- 失败时按原版语义断连：未加入 → `multiplayer.disconnect.unverified_username`，API 异常 → `multiplayer.disconnect.authservers_down`；
- 未配置 `yggdrasil` 时保留原预共享密码 + `profiles` 白名单逻辑。

#### 4. 安全模型与警告

Yggdrasil 模式的安全绑定发生在 Yggdrasil 查询里：中间人两侧分别握手时，客户端提交的 hash 和服务端查询的 hash 必然不同，`hasJoined` 返回空，连接失败；即使不固定服务端公钥也无法完成中间人。

由于这时不再使用预共享密码、也不做密码派生，控制台会在 config 加载时输出一次警告（`errors.LogWarning`）：

```text
XMC: Yggdrasil mode is enabled. The RSA key pair is generated randomly and "password"
is no longer used to derive it or to authenticate the transport; players are verified
through https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil (client /join, server /hasJoined).
Both ends must be able to reach the Yggdrasil API. The configured "password" is ignored.
```

### 兼容性

- 不配置 `yggdrasil`：完全保持旧行为（密码派生密钥 + verify to

issues.title: sockopt.interface: when the interface does not exist, the dial silently goes unbound (can loop back into TUN)
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

If an outbound has `streamSettings.sockopt.interface` set and that interface does not exist at dial time, Xray does not fail the dial. It logs `failed to apply socket options > failed to get interface ...` at **Info** level and opens the connection without any binding, so it follows the system routing table.

`transport/internet/system_dialer.go` (v26.10.10, lines 134-139; same in v26.9.9) only logs the error returned by `applyOutboundSocketOptions` and goes on to `dialer.DialContext`. The UDP path does the same (lines 77-81). The error itself comes from `net.InterfaceByName` in `transport/internet/sockopt_darwin.go:136-140`. From reading the source, Linux takes the same path (the error is logged, not returned); I tested macOS only.

Why this matters. A typical full-tunnel setup on a desktop routes everything into a TUN interface handled by Xray (default route split as 0.0.0.0/1 + 128.0.0.0/1 into the TUN), and binds outbounds with `sockopt.interface` so that their own sockets do not enter the TUN again. If the bound interface goes away, the fallback sends the outbound's sockets into the TUN, Xray routes them to the same outbound, and the connection loops.

We hit this loop in practice on macOS. A separate OpenVPN client provided a corporate network through its own utun interface, and the corporate subnet was routed to a freedom outbound so that it would follow that VPN's route. At night the OpenVPN client lost its connection and its utun interface was removed. From then on, every connection to the corporate subnet (including DNS queries to the corporate DNS server) entered the TUN, came back to the same outbound and entered the TUN again. When we looked, there were about 8,000 looped connections, all 16,384 ephemeral ports were in use, and other processes on the host got `EADDRNOTAVAIL` (`Can't assign requested address`) on connect until the loop was broken by restarting Xray.

In that incident the outbound had no `sockopt.interface` at all, so the loop itself is a config problem. The obvious fix is to bind the outbound to the other VPN's interface (`"interface": "utunN"`), so that it can never fall into the TUN. That does not work because of this issue: once the interface disappears, the binding is skipped and the loop is back. The only visible sign is an Info-level log line, which is hidden at the usual `warning` level.

Expected: if the interface named in `sockopt.interface` cannot be found, the dial fails (fail closed), as a bound socket does when its interface has no route. At the very least the error should be logged as a warning. A silent fallback to the routing table defeats the purpose of binding: it can send traffic into a tunnel (loop) or past it (leak).

### Reproduction Method

No server and no TUN are needed. Run Xray with the config below (interface `utun99` does not exist) and send a request through the SOCKS inbound:

```
curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://example.com/
```

Result: HTTP 200. The log shows that the interface was not found and the connection was opened anyway; its local endpoint is the address of whatever interface the routing table chose (on our machine, the address of a TUN interface that held the default route).

For comparison, with `"interface": "en0"` the same request goes out through en0 (local endpoint is en0's address) and no error is logged.

Expected result: the connection through the outbound bound

I think AI-assisted code review is a promising direction, and I'd like to share an example from my own experience.

I collected the history of Xray developers' discussions going back to the early days of the project, extracted key architectural decisions and the reasoning behind them, and used that material to build specialized skills and AI agents for code analysis, review, and testing.

This approach has already produced useful results. Instead of analyzing only the current source code, the agents can take the project's history, previous design decisions, and developers' experience into account when evaluating changes and designing test scenarios.

In my experience, this significantly reduces meaningless AI-generated suggestions and makes the analysis much more relevant. Of course, there is still plenty of room for improvement, and I continue refining the system for my own workflow. But the direction has proven practical.

A small part of this work is publicly available in my [Xray Core DevKit](https://github.com/svlavr/xray-core-devkit). It is more of an example of the tools and workflow than a finished universal solution.

I think we could go further and create a **publicly available AI toolkit specifically for Xray-core**, at least for preliminary PR review.

Such a toolkit could include knowledge of the project's architecture, development conventions, historical design decisions, specialized review agents, and testing procedures based on accumulated experience.

**PR authors could install this toolkit locally and run their changes through it before submitting a PR.**

This could help identify unnecessary modifications, architectural inconsistencies, compatibility issues, and common mistakes before maintainers have to review them.

Naturally, this would not replace human review or real testing. The idea is to provide a preliminary filter on the contributor's side, reducing the number of low-quality PRs and saving maintainers' time rather than creating even more AI-generated review comments for them to read.

In my opinion, the real value of AI here is not simply asking another model to review the code. With the right approach, AI could actually reduce the maintainers' workload instead of adding to it.

comments.body:
> Claude review comment:
> 
> There's a byte-order bug in `adapterGUID`: it fills `Data1`, `Data2` and `Data3` with `binary.LittleEndian`, but in a GUID's text form those three groups are the field values written most significant byte first. So the adapter gets a different GUID than the one configured:
> 
> * `"guid": "6ba7b810-9dad-11d1-80b4-00c04fd430c8"` creates the adapter as `{10B8A76B-AD9D-D111-80B4-00C04FD430C8}`
> * `"01020304-0506-0708-090a-0b0c0d0e0f10"` becomes `{04030201-0605-0807-090A-0B0C0D0E0F10}`
> 
> You can see it by comparing `adapterGUID(...).String()` with `windows.GUIDFromString("{" + guid + "}")`.
> 
> Could you please switch those three fields to `binary.BigEndian`, and update `TestAdapterGUID` to expect `Data1: 0x01020304, Data2: 0x0506, Data3: 0x0708`? Ideally the test would also check that `guid.String() == "{01020304-0506-0708-090A-0B0C0D0E0F10}"`. The MD5 fallback can stay as it is, since that GUID is never shown to anyone as text, so its byte order doesn't matter.

Thanks, you're right — fixed in the follow-up commit:
"Fix the byte order of a configured Wintun GUID".

The canonical 16 bytes keep the first three groups big-endian (that's how
`CLSIDFromString` reads them), and I was reading them with `binary.LittleEndian`,
so every group reached the adapter swapped: `01020304-0506-0708-…` landed as
`{04030201-0605-0807-…}`.

Claude review comment:

There's a byte-order bug in `adapterGUID`: it fills `Data1`, `Data2` and `Data3` with `binary.LittleEndian`, but in a GUID's text form those three groups are the field values written most significant byte first. So the adapter gets a different GUID than the one configured:

You can see it by comparing `adapterGUID(...).String()` with `windows.GUIDFromString("{" + guid + "}")`.

Could you please switch those three fields to `binary.BigEndian`, and update `TestAdapterGUID` to expect `Data1: 0x01020304, Data2: 0x0506, Data3: 0x0708`? Ideally the test would also check that `guid.String() == "{01020304-0506-0708-090A-0B0C0D0E0F10}"`. comments.body:
Hi @Fangliding, thanks for taking a look. I'd like to respectfully clarify why I believe this is not a duplicate of #6103:

- #6103 (TLS spoofing) is a fake-packet technique: it injects a forged ClientHello with a decoy SNI ahead of the real one plus TCP header manipulation - the byedpi `--fake` / zapret fake class.
- This PR is a different mechanism: the **real** ClientHello is split into segments, odd ones are sent with TTL=1 (they die on the first hop; the server recovers them via RTO retransmissions), optionally with TCP urgent data at the split boundary - the byedpi `--disorder` / `--disoob` class. There are no fake packets and no decoy SNI; what breaks is the inspector's **reassembly of the real ClientHello**.

The two techniques are complementary rather than duplicating - which is exactly why byedpi ships them as separate modes (`--fake` vs `--disorder`/`--disoob`): they solve different subtasks and are detected differently by DPI.

Also worth noting: #6103 has been a draft since May, currently has merge conflicts, and hasn't been reviewed yet, while this PR is ready for review and includes real-wire verification (tcpdump: ttl 1/64 alternation, SACK holes on server ACKs, URG flag at the split boundary).

Could you please reconsider - happy to answer any technical questions. If the concern is overlapping scope, I can split this into a feature issue for discussion instead.

comments.body:
Additional reproduction on v26.11.9 and a router-tested local mitigation

This follow-up documents TCP TLS/REALITY setup stalls reproduced against v26.11.9, an experimental local patch, and measurements from a memory-constrained router. The failure mechanism overlaps the one described in this issue.

The test device was a **Keenetic Giga (KN-1012) EAEU**, with 512 MB nominal RAM, KeeneticOS 5.02.B.4.0-0, Entware aarch64, and XKeen 2.1. The original Xray binary reported v26.11.9, commit 676eaf6, built with go1.27.3 for linux/arm64. The local patched build used the v26.11.9 source tag and go1.27.0.

The production setup had 37 outbounds, mostly VLESS over TCP with REALITY, plus burstObservatory and multiple balancers. Unresponsive peers produced recurring probe timeouts. Symptoms included intermittent Internet failures and periods when the router management interface stopped responding.

| Observation before the source patch | Xray RSS | Xray open file descriptors | System MemAvailable |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| About five minutes after router startup | 76.3 MiB | 596 | 151.7 MiB |
| About thirteen minutes after startup, same process | 134.5 MiB | 1,469 | 78.8 MiB |
| Later run after several hours, with GOMEMLIMIT=96MiB and a 30s probe interval | 109.5 MiB | 8,401 | 37.9 MiB |

A soft Go memory limit and less frequent probes left file-descriptor accumulation observable. The cause of the earlier router restart remains uncertain. The retained router logs contained no OOM-killer record. The measurements point to accumulating connection resources alongside memory pressure.

In transport/internet/tcp/dialer.go at v26.11.9, TLS/REALITY negotiation uses the supplied context. A long-lived context can leave negotiation pending against a peer that accepts TCP and then stops responding. Several unsuccessful setup paths also return without explicitly closing the original socket. The change below keeps a reference to that socket, closes it on unsuccessful setup, and applies an eight-second socket deadline during TLS/REALITY negotiation. The deadline is cleared when Dial returns after successful setup.

**Eight seconds is the timeout chosen for this local build.** It bounds negotiation after the underlying TCP connection is established. TCP establishment has its own dialer timeout. The setup deadline is removed for an established connection. A configurable timeout and review of context cancellation would be appropriate considerations for an upstream implementation.

<details>
<summary>Experimental patch against v26.11.9</summary>

```diff
--- a/transport/internet/tcp/dialer.go
+++ b/transport/internet/tcp/dialer.go
@@ -5,6 +5,7 @@
 	gotls "crypto/tls"
 	"slices"
 	"strings"
+	"time"
 
 	"github.com/xtls/xray-core/common"
 	"github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/errors"
@@ -30,6 +31,22 @@
 		return nil, errors.New("failed to dial to dest").Base(err)
 	}
 
+	// Bound TLS/REALITY negotiation and release the original socket on every
+	// failed setup path, including health checks whose request has timed out.
+	rawConn := conn
+	setupComplete := false
+	defer func() {
+		if !setupComplete {
```

comments.body:
Looked at the TUN code on current main (02cf0f6) to see where the ordering comes from.

The SYN-ACK goes out as soon as the SYN comes in (`stack.handleTCP` → `sendSyn`, stack.go:354). `HandleConnection` only starts once the final ACK arrives (tcp_lightweight.go:521), so by the time routing/dial happens the app's `connect()` has already returned success.

When the dial then fails, nothing tells the TUN side directly: the outbound's `Interrupt(link.Writer)` is a no-op on `TCPWriter`, and `DispatchLink` returns nil regardless (default.go:324-376). The conn just gets closed by `HandleConnection`'s deferred `conn.Close()`, which sends a FIN, or an RST if the client already sent data nobody read (tcp_lightweight.go:1230-1236). Either way the app gets it after a successful connect, so nothing at that point makes it fall back to v4.

Delaying the SYN-ACK until the outbound is up wouldn't work with sniffing on either (unless `metadataOnly`): `DispatchLink` reads the first bytes from the client before routing (default.go:350), and the client only sends them after the handshake. Same chicken-and-egg as the ALPN thing you mentioned.

Only read the code, I haven't run this on a real TUN with a v4-only physical interface.

issues.title: fix: find the Linux default gateway when the route table is larger than 8 KB
issues.body:
## Summary

- Parse the netlink route dump in `NetworkUtilities::getGatewayAndIface()` one datagram at a time instead of collecting it into a fixed 8 KB buffer, so the default gateway is found whatever the size of the routing table.
- Request IPv4 routes only and stop at the first main-table route that has a gateway and an interface.
- Zero-initialize the receive timeout and close the netlink socket on every return path.

Fixes #3090. #2997 and #3244 report the same `No default gateway available, skipping exclusion route` symptom.

## Root cause

`getGatewayAndIface()` sends an `RTM_GETROUTE` dump request for all address families, appends every reply datagram to an 8 KB stack buffer and parses it only after `NLMSG_DONE`. The kernel splits the dump into several datagrams. Once the total is over 8 KB (a bit over a hundred routes on a typical desktop), `recv()` truncates a datagram or is called with no space left, `NLMSG_OK` fails and the function returns an empty gateway after `Error in received packet`.

`LinuxRouteMonitor::rtmSendRoute()` needs this gateway for every exclusion (`RTN_THROW`) route, both to add and to delete it. So once the table is that large:

- in the "all except sites" split tunneling mode every added exclusion grows the table, and after roughly the first hundred entries the rest are skipped;
- the exclusions that were added cannot be deleted on disconnect and stay in the main table until reboot;
- on the next connection the table is too large from the start, the exclusion for the server endpoint is skipped as well, and WireGuard packets to the server are routed into the tunnel. A leftover exclusion keeps the previous server working, while switching to another server breaks (#2997).

`struct timeval tv` also had an uninitialized `tv_usec`, so `setsockopt(SO_RCVTIMEO)` could fail with `EDOM` (`Error in received packet: Numerical argument out of domain` in the log), and the socket leaked on every early return.

## Compared with the open PRs

- #3170 raises the buffer to 128 KB and #3231 to 64 KB, but both still collect the whole dump before parsing it, so a larger table (long split tunneling lists, many container networks) fails the same way. Here each datagram is parsed as it arrives, in a 32 KB buffer, the size the kernel caps dump datagrams at, so there is no limit on the table size.
- #3470 reads `/proc/net/route` instead of netlink. This PR keeps netlink and the structure of the function.
- `addExclusionRoute()` calls this function once per exclusion. Stopping at the first route with a gateway, which in practice is in the first datagram, means that with long lists each call no longer re-reads a table that keeps growing.

## Validation

- Built the function into a small test program and ran it against a real routing table with a long split tunneling list (a route dump of about 9 KB): the current code prints `Error in received packet` and returns no gateway, the new code returns the default gateway.
- In a network namespace (`unshare -rn`) with a veth pair, a default route and extra `/32` routes: the current code fails at 1,004 routes, the new code finds the gateway at 20,004 routes.
- Built the Linux client with this change and connected with about 750 split tunneling entries: the endpoint exclusion and all site exclusions are installed, `ip route get <endpoint>` goes through the physical gateway, and the delete requests on disconnect get the gateway too.
- `clang-format` on the changed lines.

issues.title: Windows: Full-tunnel route capture overrides connected routes on other interfaces
issues.body:
## Description

In Windows full-tunnel mode (VpnAllSites), AmneziaVPN clones routes from other network interfaces onto the VPN interface. This includes directly connected networks used by virtual networking systems such as Windows HNS.

The cloned routes can override the original routes, causing Windows to send traffic to local networks through the VPN interface instead of the interface that owns those networks. This breaks connectivity to HNS container networks, including return traffic.

## Environment
- AmneziaVPN 5.1.0.6
- Windows
- Full-tunnel mode (VpnAllSites)
- Split tunneling disabled
- Windows HNS NAT container network

## Steps to reproduce
1. Create and start a Windows HNS NAT container network.
2. Verify the connected route to the HNS subnet through the HNS virtual Ethernet interface.
3. Connect AmneziaVPN in full-tunnel mode with split tunneling disabled.
4. Inspect the IPv4 routing table and run Find-NetRoute for an address in the HNS subnet.

## Observed behavior
The same route 10.250.0.0/24 is present on two interfaces:
- AmneziaVPN, ifIndex 30, metric 0.
- HNS vEthernet NAT, ifIndex 96, metric 256.

Find-NetRoute selects the AmneziaVPN interface instead of HNS for destinations in this subnet.

The same behavior was observed for other connected networks: 172.26.144.0/20, 192.168.56.0/24, and 192.168.88.0/24.

This can cause traffic destined for local virtual networks to be sent through the VPN interface, breaking container connectivity.

## Expected behavior
Full-tunnel route capture should preserve routes to directly connected networks on other interfaces. Traffic destined for an HNS container network should continue to use the HNS interface, while Internet-bound traffic continues to use the VPN.

## Relevant implementation
In WindowsRouteMonitor::updateCapturedRoutes() in windowsroutemonitor.cpp, eligible routes are cloned onto the VPN interface. The observed behavior suggests that connected routes belonging to other interfaces are not excluded.

WireguardUtilsWindows::updateRoutePrefix() enables default-route capture when a 0.0.0.0/0 route is installed.

This behavior was reproduced with split tunneling disabled, so it is not limited to the split-tunneling scenario in issue #2830.

Related issue: https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/issues/2830

issues.title: [macOS] Export/Share config fails with Error 224 when VPN connection is active (NetworkExtension routing loop?)
issues.body:
## 🐞 Description
After a recent macOS update, the Amnezia VPN client (v5.1.1.10) fails to export or share the XRay configuration while the VPN connection to the server is active. It throws an **Error 224**.

This appears to be a regression or a `NetworkExtension` routing conflict specific to macOS, where the application cannot query its own server API through its own active tunnel.

## 🔄 Steps to Reproduce
1. Install Amnezia VPN (v5.1.1.10) on macOS.
2. Add a self-hosted server and install the **XRay** protocol.
3. Connect to the VPN (status: *Connected*).
4. Click on the server -> **"Share"** or **"Export"** configuration.

## ✅ Expected Behavior
The app successfully requests a new config from the server API and displays the QR code / config file, exactly as it does when the VPN connection is turned off.

## ❌ Actual Behavior
The action fails with an error (e.g., `"ErrorCode: 224"` or `"XRay is not accepting connections..."`).

## 💻 Environment
- **OS:** macOS 27.2.1 (26B131)
- **Chip / Architecture:** Apple Silicon (M1) *(или укажи M2/M3/Intel, если другой)*
- **App Version:** 5.1.1.10
- **Protocol:** XRay
- **Server OS:** Ubuntu (clean install on Timeweb Cloud)

## 🔍 Additional Context & Diagnostics
I performed local network diagnostics to isolate the root cause. The issue is **not** related to the server, ISP, or DPI blocking.

- **Server is healthy:** `tcpdump` on the Ubuntu server confirms that the TCP handshake (ACK) is successful. The server receives the API request from the macOS client and sends response packets back.
- **Local macOS drop:** Despite the server responding, the macOS client never receives the payload, indicating the response is dropped or misrouted locally.

### Workarounds
1. **Workaround 1 (Proves local routing issue):** If I turn the Amnezia VPN **OFF** before clicking "Share/Export", the action succeeds instantly (the request goes through the standard Wi-Fi interface, bypassing the `utun` tunnel).
2. **Workaround 2 (Proves tunnel conflict):** If I activate a different, third-party VPN on macOS, the Amnezia export function works perfectly. This confirms that the third-party tunnel bypasses Amnezia's broken `utun` routing rules.

## 💡 Hypothesis & Proposed Fix
When the Amnezia tunnel is active, the macOS `NetworkExtension` framework does not properly exclude the app's own internal API requests from the VPN routing table. This creates a routing loop or causes the macOS packet filter (`pf`) to silently drop the response packets destined for the app itself.

**Suggestion:** Please consider adding a split-tunneling exception for the app's own API endpoints or fixing the `utun` routing behavior on recent macOS versions.
